Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Samson’s Take: Galamsey – we know the kingpins, so why pretend? Source : Myjoyonline 28 November 2026 9:24am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Last Saturday, I asked how many more rivers must be poisoned? How many more forests destroyed? How many more children exposed to toxic dangers? And how many more security officers ought to be attacked and killed before Ghana confronts the truth about Galamsey?
We recalled the long and exhausting catalogue of interventions, Operation Vanguard, Operation Halt 1 and 2, among others, soldiers, drones, and now NAIMOS being attacked by a militia. We remembered Major Maxwell Adam Mahama, brutally murdered in 2017, and recounted the attacks on enforcement personnel and the growing danger of armed criminal networks challenging the authority of the state.
But there is another tragedy we must never forget. Eight precious Ghanaian lives. On 6 August 2025, a military helicopter carrying eight Ghanaians to Obuasi crashed.
They were traveling for the launch of a program to combat illegal mining and promote responsible livelihoods. Among them were two of my very good friends, Defense Minister Dr. Edward Omane Boamah and Environment Minister Dr. Ibrahim Murtala Mohammed. Eight Ghanaian citizens lost, eight families bereaved, and a nation was plunged into mourning.
And what have we learned? Nothing. What have we changed? Nothing. Must Ghana continue to pay such a terrible price while those who profit most from galamsey escape accountability? Who are we really fighting? When the cameras arrive at an illegal mining pit, whose face do we see? The muddy, exhausted young man standing waist deep in polluted water.
When arrests are announced, whose names do we hear? The diggers, the laborers, the desperate young men whose poverty makes them visible, vulnerable, and replaceable. But did that young man buy that expensive excavator? Did he finance the machinery, purchase the fuel, hire the guards, or secure the political connections? Where is the owner? Where is the financier? Where is the powerful protector? Where are they? We arrest the hungry and leave those who feed on their hunger to count their fortunes. Research by CDD Ghana, involving a ... William Nyako, identified nine financiers associated with illicit activities, seven of whom were linked to illegal mining, political financiers.
Seven out of nine think about the implications for our politics. The criminal economy finances political ambition. Political ambition produces public officials, and those officials are expected to destroy the very criminal economy that may have financed their rise to power.
What an extraordinary contradiction. And have we not seen what is happening in our political parties? Television sets, refrigerators, blenders, cars, motorcycles, pickup trucks distributed to influence delegates. The NDC's own investigations into the Baba Jamal parliamentary primary found widespread inducement and vote buying, yet the winner remained a candidate.
The NDP's primaries have equally generated reports of cash payments and inducements. Different party colours, the same troubling political culture. Why do people spend fortunes seeking party offices or positions that may not even attract salaries? Yes, they don't attract salaries, so let's pretend we don't know why they want to kill for those offices.
Is it love for the party, public service, or political power is an investment from which candidates and their financiers expect returns, appointments, contracts, influence, and protection. How can politicians who depend on questionable money to acquire power be expected to fight the corruption that produces that money? And what of the enforcers?
In my work as a journalist, I've encountered disturbing accounts of the sudden wealth of some district officials, I'm talking about DCEs in Galamsey areas, and allegations of security personnel enriching themselves through anti-galamsey assignments. Some even compete for these deployments.
So who is auditing the enforcer? Who is investigating the investigator? Fellow ghanaians, let's stop counting only the excavators burnt, and the poor miners arrested tell us how many financiers have been prosecuted, how many beneficial owners identified, how many corrupt officials convicted, how many criminal wealth recovered, and how many rivers restored.
That's what we want to know. That's what we want to see. That's all we want to hear. What credible alternative livelihood have we provided for the hungry young man whom the wealthy financier will simply replace tomorrow? You arrest them in the thousands and throw them in. That's it. They will be replaced.
We have lost too much. Our rivers, our forests, the safety of our food, the health of our children, and the precious lives of people serving this republic. Eight gallant citizens perished while traveling on a mission connected with this national struggle.
And still, the criminal economy survives. What more must Ghana sacrifice? The danger is no longer merely environmental destruction. It is illicit wealth corrupting our politics, compromising law enforcement, financing armed resistance.
That's why those guys can look into the faces of military people and shoot at them. And it's weakening the authority of the state. We cannot save Ghana by arresting only the hungry man in the pits.
We must follow the money, find the owners, expose the financiers, investigate the political protectors, prosecute the corrupt provider in the process, and provide genuine alternatives for the desperate young people they are exploiting. Our rivers are dying. Our people have died.
Our future is at stake. We know the kingpins. We know them. Mr. President, we know them. You say, why do we pretend? And that would be my take.
